tldr: A framework that enables coordinated whole-body loco-manipulation (including closing a drawer with a foot) without robot teleoperation data, using coarse-to-fine offline action alignment and visual adaptation on egocentric data collected from wearable human sensors.
hero_caption: Hardware setup of the wearable human capture system (GoPro, PICO headset and trackers) and the physical humanoid robot (Unitree G1 with BrainCo Revo2 hands). First-person images, hand poses, and whole-body motions are mapped to each other, training policies through both visual and action alignment.
overview:
When teaching humanoid robots complex whole-body loco-manipulation, the biggest bottleneck is collecting high-quality motion data. Robot teleoperation is tedious and costly. Meanwhile, prior methods relying on human egocentric data often depended on decoupled control—separating upper-body manipulation from lower-body locomotion—making it difficult to directly transfer dynamic skills where the entire body moves in concert.

To solve this, the authors propose EgoHumanoid-V2, a framework that directly transfers coordinated whole-body skills to humanoids from first-person human demonstrations. At its heart is coarse-to-fine action alignment. First, it uses offline inverse kinematics (IK) to roughly correct geometric mismatches between the robot's reference motion and the human. Next, using a learned local response model and simulator rollout feedback, it iteratively minimizes tracking errors at the end-effectors without disrupting the whole-body tracker's balance. Furthermore, replacing human arms with rendered robot arms alongside image augmentation bridges the visual embodiment gap.

Evaluated on four real-world tasks using a physical humanoid (Unitree G1)—closing a laptop, opening a fridge, pulling a curtain, and pushing a drawer shut with a foot—VLA (Vision-Language-Action) policies trained solely on aligned human data achieved the tasks without any real-robot demonstrations. The data collection cost was reduced by about 76% compared to teleoperation, demonstrating that human data can serve as highly effective, direct skill supervision.
contributions: Built the first framework for directly transferring coordinated whole-body loco-manipulation skills from egocentric human demonstrations to humanoid robots.

Proposed a coarse-to-fine action alignment method combining geometric correction with dynamics-aware iterative refinement, improving end-effector accuracy while preserving the whole-body controller's balance.
Demonstrated zero-shot skill transfer without real-robot teleoperation data across four real-world tasks using hands and feet on a physical humanoid (Unitree G1).
Quantitatively showed a 76.36% reduction in data collection cost (person-hours) compared to teleoperation while achieving performance on par with policies trained on teleoperation data.

sections.heading: Why Is Coordinated Whole-Body Skill Transfer So Hard?
sections.summary: Transferring coordinated whole-body skills to humanoids requires more than just tracking end-effector trajectories. This chapter highlights the fundamental issue of online end-effector IK destabilizing whole-body tracking controllers, introducing the paper's concept of offline coarse-to-fine action alignment.
sections.details:
Humans naturally coordinate their torso and legs alongside their arms and hands to expand their workspace and perform tasks efficiently. However, transferring such whole-body coordination to humanoid robots is challenging.

Most prior egocentric transfer studies adopted decoupled control, treating upper-body manipulation independently from lower-body locomotion and balance. In contrast, recent whole-body tracking policies generate all joint commands simultaneously from full-body state feedback, enabling rich coordinated motions. Yet, tracking raw human reference motions directly often leads to significant end-effector positioning errors.

One might think: "Why not just solve IK online to adjust the end-effector commands?" But overwriting part of a coupled whole-body command with online IK breaks the controller's overall balance, risking robot falls (which occurred frequently in the authors' experiments).

Here is the key question: how can we improve end-effector interaction accuracy while maintaining full-body balance and coordination? To solve this dilemma, the authors developed EgoHumanoid-V2, combining coarse-to-fine offline action alignment with visual alignment.

sections.heading: Prior Approaches to Whole-Body Control and Human Demonstrations
sections.summary: This section reviews whole-body control for loco-manipulation and previous methods for learning robot policies from human demonstrations. The key distinction of this work is offline optimization of action labels under a fixed whole-body tracker without retraining controllers per task.
sections.details:
Prior research related to this work broadly falls into two lines of study.

### 2.1 Whole-Body Control
Controllers for whole-body humanoid control have advanced through imitation learning and teleoperation. For loco-manipulation, some approaches separate arm IK from adaptive leg locomotion, while whole-body tracking policies handle diverse motions within a single control system. However, structural embodiment differences leave tracking errors, leading to attempts like residual learning. This work keeps the base whole-body controller (SONIC) fixed across tasks, instead refining the input reference trajectories and tokens offline.

### 2.2 Learning from Human Demonstrations
Methods learning representations or latent action models from human videos, as well as setups like UMI that directly capture hand trajectories as robot supervision, have grown rapidly. Recently, egocentric whole-body imitation has also been studied, but most still rely on decoupled control. This work sets itself apart by refining the action labels offline under a fixed tracker, turning human demonstrations into direct supervision for coordinated whole-body behavior.

sections.heading: Bridging Action and Appearance Gaps with Two Pipelines
sections.summary: This section details the action alignment and visual alignment pipelines that convert human demonstration data into training data for VLA models. Coarse geometric correction (K), iterative refinement via a response model (D), 3D arm rendering, and image augmentations enable zero-shot real-robot execution.
sections.details:
The overall workflow consists of data collection, action alignment, and visual alignment.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Hardware Setup
The human capture system uses a GoPro (a neck-mounted first-person RGB camera) and a PICO 4 Ultra (full-body motion capture using 5 trackers on the head, wrists, and ankles), recorded synchronously at 50 Hz. The target deployment robot is a Unitree G1 equipped with a head-mounted GoPro and BrainCo Revo2 hands.

### 3.2 Policy Learning Framework
The policy uses $\pi_{0.5}$, a VLA model. Its inputs are the adapted first-person image $\widetilde{I}_t$, the robot's 43-dimensional proprioceptive state $q_t$, and a language instruction $\ell$. Its outputs are a 64-dimensional motion token $z_t$ fed into the whole-body tracker (SONIC), along with 6-dimensional open/close commands $h_t^{\mathrm{L}/R}$ for the left and right hands.

### 3.3 Coarse-to-Fine Action Alignment
Feeding human motions directly into the tracker leaves noticeable tracking errors. Action alignment is therefore performed in stages (Figure F3 (a)):
- **Initialization ($H$)**: The human whole-body motion is tracked by SONIC in simulation to obtain an initial robot trajectory.
- **Kinematic Reference Correction ($K$)**: To reduce geometric discrepancies with the target end-effector poses, constrained offline IK modifies the joint reference trajectory, which is then re-encoded into motion tokens.
- **Dynamics-Aware Refinement ($D$)**: Even after $K$, execution errors remain due to controller dynamics. The pipeline combines rollout feedback with a local response model $\mathcal{R}_\psi$ parameterized by an MLP. This MLP predicts how token changes affect executed end-effector positions. Rather than differentiating through the simulator, gradients flow through this MLP to iteratively optimize motion tokens and cancel out end-effector tracking residuals.

### 3.4 Visual Alignment
Two techniques bridge the gap in appearance and perspective (Figure F3 (b)):
- **Robot Arm Rendering**: Human forearms and trackers are segmented using SAM2 and background-inpainted with DiffuEraser. Rendered G1 robot arms are then composited in place based on the aligned joint poses.
- **Image Augmentation**: Random cropping, rotation, and color jittering are applied to enhance robustness against viewpoint differences caused by human head sway and robot walking oscillations.

captions.F3: Overall pipeline of action and visual alignment. (a) Human motion (H) undergoes geometric correction via offline IK (K), followed by iterative refinement via an MLP response model (D) to generate accurate motion. (b) Human forearms are masked and inpainted, and rendered robot arms are composited to bridge the embodiment appearance gap.

sections.heading: Real Humanoid Experiments: How Far Can It Go Without Teleoperation?
sections.summary: Using a physical Unitree G1 robot, performance was evaluated across four coordinated tasks including foot manipulation. With 200 human demonstrations, the policy achieved an average success score of 51.67%, cutting collection costs by 76% while approaching policies trained on teleoperation data.
sections.details:
The authors evaluated their framework on a physical Unitree G1 across four tasks requiring hand-foot coordination.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The four evaluation tasks are:
1. **Close Laptop**: Reach out with the right hand and press down the laptop screen (end-effector positioning and contact force control).
2. **Open Fridge**: Hook the left hand into the fridge door seam and pull it open (sustained contact under posture change).
3. **Pull Curtain**: Grasp the curtain and pull it sideways by 1 meter (coordinating walking with arm pulling).
4. **Close Drawer**: Raise the right foot and push an open drawer shut using the toe (single-leg balance and foot positioning).
Each task was tested over 20 real-robot trials, scoring progress across three sub-steps (0, 33.3, 66.7, 100%) and averaging the results.

### 4.2 Q1: Skill Transfer from Human Demonstrations
Trained on 200 human demonstrations per task, the policy achieved an average score of 51.67% across all four tasks through zero-shot transfer without any real-robot demonstrations (Figure F4). Increasing demonstrations from 25 to 200 steadily raised the average score from 38.33% to 51.67%, confirming that data scaling helps.

### 4.3 Q2: Human Data vs. Robot Teleoperation Data
On Close Laptop and Pull Curtain, policies trained on 200 human demonstrations scored 53.33% each, approaching policies trained on 50 teleoperation demonstrations (63.33% and 56.67%). The collection labor cost (person-seconds) reveals an even bigger advantage: teleoperation required two people (an operator and a resetter) averaging 140.85 seconds per episode, whereas wearable human capture needed only one person and took 33.30 seconds on average—a 76.36% reduction. For equivalent labor time, collecting human data is far more efficient.

### 4.4 Q3: Effectiveness of Action Alignment
The initial state ($H$) had end-effector errors of 11.21 cm in position and 21.22° in orientation. Geometric correction ($K$) reduced these to 4.45 cm / 13.77°, and iterative refinement ($D_s$) brought them down to 3.41 cm / 6.71°. Real-robot task scores also rose clearly: 21.25% ($H$) $\to$ 47.08% ($H+K$) $\to$ 51.67% ($H+K+D_s$). As shown in Figure F6, repeating $K$ alone quickly plateaus in position accuracy, but applying $D$ iteratively after $K$ dramatically improves precision.

### 4.5 Q4: Effectiveness of Visual Alignment
Applying both arm rendering and image augmentation raised the average score across the three arm-manipulation tasks from a 38.89% baseline to 48.33%. This confirms that bridging the appearance gap is vital for policy learning.

captions.F4: Human demonstrations (top), robot execution (middle), and task scores across demonstration counts from 25 to 200 (bottom) on the four real-world tasks. Zero-shot transfer from human data alone succeeds even on foot drawer closing (Close Drawer), with scores improving as demonstration volume scales up.
captions.F6: Relationship between iteration depth of K (kinematic correction) and D (dynamics refinement) and end-effector errors during action alignment. Repeating K alone (dashed blue line) plateaus quickly, but applying D iteratively after a single K pass (solid green line, KD^k) significantly reduces both position and orientation errors.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook
sections.summary: EgoHumanoid-V2 achieved zero-shot transfer of coordinated whole-body loco-manipulation without real-robot teleoperation, thanks to coarse-to-fine action alignment and visual adaptation. Future directions include speeding up optimization and strengthening stability constraints.
sections.details:
EgoHumanoid-V2 realized direct transfer of coordinated whole-body skills from human first-person demonstrations to humanoids. By combining geometric reference correction with dynamics-aware refinement offline, the framework dramatically improved end-effector interaction accuracy without compromising controller balance.

### Limitations and Future Work
Current limitations include occasional generation of unstable motions during the alignment process and the computational time required for repeated IK solving and simulation rollouts. Incorporating stronger stability constraints and accelerating optimization throughput will be key topics for future research.

sections.heading: Appendix: Why Online IK Fails and Offline Refinement Is Essential
sections.summary: This appendix covers why directly embedding online IK into whole-body trackers frequently causes falls (Appendix D) and presents multi-task validation (Appendix C). It highlights the dangers of overriding end-effector poses while ignoring full-body dynamic coupling.
sections.details:
The appendix reports key additional experiments supporting the proposed approach.

### Failure of Direct Online IK Correction (Appendix D)
To address the question: "Why not apply IK corrections directly to the joints during online execution?", the authors evaluated three variants (A: no balance correction, B: additive SONIC balance correction, C: restricted IK joints). Across all 60 trials, unstable behavior occurred. In the foot drawer-closing task, all 15 trials fell during the initial posture phase (Figures F8–F10). Overwriting parts of the coordinated commands generated by the whole-body tracker disrupts ground reaction forces and base dynamic coupling. This outcome strongly justifies refining tokens offline outside the controller loop.

### Generalization of Action Alignment Across 50 Tasks (Appendix C)
Beyond the four main real-world tasks, large-scale simulation tests were conducted across 50 tasks and 112 trajectories (Figure F7). Here too, tracking errors dropped progressively from 17.03 cm ($H$) to 5.22 cm ($K$) and 3.83 cm ($D$), demonstrating the robustness of the proposed coarse-to-fine pipeline.

captions.F7: Iteration depth versus tracking error on the extended 50-task benchmark. As in the 4-task experiments, pairing one pass of K with repeated D iterations (KD^k) reduces end-effector position and orientation errors most efficiently and accurately.
captions.F8: Failure case of online IK Variant A (no balance correction). Forcing end-effector position corrections via online IK disrupted whole-body dynamic balance, causing severe tilting, tracking failure, and falls.
captions.F10: Fall sequence under online IK Variant C (restricting joints modified by IK). Even when limiting affected joints, dynamic coordination with the lower body was broken, ultimately resulting in the robot falling completely.

takeaways: Overriding commands with online end-effector IK on a whole-body tracking controller destroys balance and causes falls; refining controller input tokens offline is far more effective.

For action alignment, a pipeline running a single pass of coarse kinematic correction (K) followed by multiple rounds of response-model dynamics refinement (D) yields the best trade-off between precision and computational efficiency.

Egocentric human demonstrations can serve as direct supervision for zero-shot transfer of coordinated whole-body skills—including contact manipulation with feet (such as closing drawers)—without requiring physical robot demonstrations.
Collecting human demonstrations with wearable sensors reduces person-hour costs by roughly 76% compared to robot teleoperation, offering a powerful tool for data scaling.
limitations: Iterative simulation rollouts and local optimization during action alignment incur significant offline computational overhead and time.
Unstable motions are still occasionally produced during optimization, pointing to a need for stricter fall-prevention constraints and better trajectory filtering.
Policies were evaluated per task (one policy trained per task); complete multi-task generalization to unseen environments under a single unified VLA policy remains to be validated.
